headlines.title: Trump administration sues California to block state from counting alleged noncitizen mail-in ballots
headlines.description: The Trump administration sued California election officials Thursday, asking a judge to bar the state from counting mail-in ballots for next month’s midterm elections from people the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed. The lawsuit comes after the Justice Department said California officials failed to meet a 48-hour deadline to review a password-protected thumb drive that contains a list of 20,000 names. The federal government says those are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election, although the secretary of state said the administration has provided no evidence to support that claim. The state mails ballots to all registered voters. The lawsuit follows a letter sent earlier this week by a top Justice Department official who threatened potential legal action if California didn’t comply. The federal government didn’t specify where the 20,000 voters were concentrated, but the list was sent directly to Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan on Tuesday, his office confirmed in a statement. Logan is also named as a defendant in the lawsuit. The county has roughly 6 million voters, roughly half of whom are registered Democrats, according to the secretary of state’s office. Over 23 million people are registered statewide, and there are a handful of competitive congressional races in other California districts that could determine which party has control of the U.S. House for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term. Expert says lawsuit could set stage for false election claims California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in a letter to the Justice Department that the federal government hasn’t provided evidence to support its allegation that 20,000 names on the state’s voter rolls are of noncitizens. She referenced an instance in which the federal government initially alleged nearly 16,000 possible noncitizens were listed on Nevada’s voter rolls, but the state determined that all the people flagged were, in fact, U.S. citizens. She also noted that voting is already underway in the state. Weber, a Democrat, said the Justice Department was “demanding unprecedented measures that threaten thousands of Californians’ right to vote, based on unverifiable information or methodology that you still fail to explain or provide.” California’s elections are in “full compliance” with federal law, she added. David Becker, an election law expert who heads the Center for Election Innovation and Research, called the Justice Department’s lawsuit “fairly frivolous.” “If they were seeking to work in good faith to clean up the voter list that they believed had issues, they would have done this months ago in a much different fashion,” Becker said. “However, it does raise questions as to whether or not the sole purpose of this is to set the stage for false claims about elections.” List of alleged illegal voters delivered on a thumb drive Logan said his office received the thumb drive along with a “hand written note providing a password” to access the list of alleged noncitizens on the voter rolls. He said he did not consider the thumb drive a secure device. The secretary of state’s office said the password was written “on a sticky note.” Becker said most election officials’ cybersecurity protocols would not allow them to comply with the Justice Department’s request as it was sent. “Election offices do not just stick thumb drives into their technology, for very good reason,” he said. The Justice Department’s lawsuit says the federal government sought to “work collaboratively” with California to identify noncitizens registered to vote in the state, and “California made no serious effort to do so.” “The United States thus seeks commonplace election relief when a ballot is called into question,” the lawsuit says. “This Court should enjoin California from presently tabulating vote by-mail ballots from likely noncitizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter’s citizenship status can be determined,” the lawsuit says. Weber, who is named in the lawsuit, suggested the federal government’s outreach had not been collaborative. She said that over the summer, the Department of Homeland Security claimed that California had 190,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls but refused to provide the methodology or data sources when the office asked for them. In her letter Thursday, she called the recent demands “an emergency of the DOJ’s creation.” Letters sent weeks before elections The letter sent by acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter gave the state 48 hours to research the list of the 20,000 people it claims might not be citizens. For those whose citizenship cannot be independently verified, the state is to instruct local election officials to segregate their mail-in ballots until their immigration status can be determined, and to not provide a ballot to anyone who has not yet received one. California Attorney General Rob Bonta said at an unrelated press conference Thursday morning that state officials would not carry out the federal government’s requests to withhold ballots for the alleged noncitizen voters. He noted that the administration’s alleged number of noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls had dropped from the 190,000 flagged over the summer by the Department of Homeland Security to the 20,000 noted by the Justice Department. “What happened to those 170,000? They just got those wrong,” Bonta said. He also said the Trump administration was violating a federal law that prohibits states from changing voter rolls within 90 days of an election. “They are in unprecedented, baseless, lawless territory,” he said. The Trump administration has made the hunt for noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though the problem is exceptionally rare. The Justice Department has charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election. Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, defended the Justice Department’s move to take California to court. “This is not political or controversial,” he wrote in a post on X. “We will not allow California to dilute the votes of American citizens.” ___ Austin reported from Sacramento, Riddle from Los Angeles and Durkin Richer from Washington. Associated Press writer Ali Swenson in New York contributed. .
headlines.source: Alanna Durkin Richer | The Associated Press, Sophie Austin | The Associated Press and Safiyah Riddle | The Associated Press

headlines.title: Lanes of Highway 101 at Hospital Curve in San Francisco to close this weekend
headlines.description: All southbound lanes and one northbound lane of Highway 101 at Hospital Curve in San Francisco will be closed this weekend for an ongoing construction project. The closure between Cesar Chavez Street and 17th Street will start at 11 p.m. Friday and continue until 6 a.m. Monday, according to Caltrans. Motorists should avoid the area and consider taking Interstate 280 as an alternate, Caltrans said. This marks the third closure for the ongoing Hospital Curve repaving and rehabilitation project, which started last fall. The fourth and final closure – impacting the same lanes as this weekend’s closure – is scheduled for the weekend of Nov. 6-9, weather permitting, according to Caltrans.

headlines.title: Elderly woman seriously injured in San Francisco hit and run involving e-bike
headlines.description: A hit-and-run collision involving an electric bicycle seriously injured an 88-year-old woman on Upper Market Street in San Francisco on Wednesday evening, according to police. The collision was reported at about 5:30 p.m. in the area of Market and Church streets. San Francisco police said the woman was crossing the street when a bicyclist hit her and then fled the scene. The woman was taken to a hospital with life-threatening injuries and an update on her condition was not immediately available Thursday. No arrest has been made in the case and police have not shared any details about the suspect or bicycle. Anyone with information about the collision is asked to call the SFPD tip line at 415-575-4444 or to send a tip by text message to TIP411 with “SFPD” at the start of the message.

headlines.title: Bay Area features in top 10 of WalletHub's greenest cities in America
headlines.description: Multiple cities in the Bay Area and Northern California were named in WalletHub’s 2026 Greenest Cities in America list. Oakland, San Jose and San Francisco were the top three cities on the list, respectively, while Fremont was placed seventh. WalletHub’s ranking was composed of 100 cities in the U.S. compared on metrics of environment, transportation, energy sources, and lifestyle and policy. Oakland has the second-lowest greenhouse gas emissions and the best air quality in the country, alongside the lowest light pollution levels in the country. The city also has the 30th-highest percentage of designated parkland among the 100 cities in WalletHub’s list with 12%. In addition, Oakland has the 20th-most bicycle lanes and paths, a high number of community garden sites and farmers’ markets, and ranked 24th in most green job openings per capita. San Jose boasts the fifth-highest number of solar panel installations per capita and the fifth-highest percentage of electricity coming from renewable sources at 50%. San Jose also has the fourth-lowest Urban Heat Island Effect Index in the country, with the use of green energy in the city helping to keep it from being an excessively hot environment. San Jose also bans plastic bags, has a bike-sharing program and employs many initiatives that promote the use of green energy. San Francisco’s approach to locally sourced food helped it reach top three in WalletHub’s list. It leads the country in Community Supported Agriculture (CSA) groups and community garden sites per capita. It also has the fourth-most farmers’ markets per capita. Like San Jose, San Francisco gets more than 50% of its energy from renewable sources, the fifth-highest percentage in the country. Residents’ water conservation efforts placed San Francisco at the ninth-lowest daily water consumption per capita in the country. San Francisco also has the 13th-most alternative-fuel stations for vehicles and the 20th-most solar panel installations per capita. The city is also ranked fourth in transportation for the low percentage of commuters who drive to work by themselves. While Fremont was seventh overall, the city was joint-ranked first for environment and energy sources. The city issued a statement saying the ranking was the result of a strong commitment to reducing greenhouse gas emissions, preserving ample green space and advancements in renewable energy. Stockton was ranked 27th in WalletHub’s 100 greenest cities list and joint-first in energy sources.

headlines.title: Average long-term US mortgage rate holds at 7.4%, remaining at highest level in nearly 3 years
headlines.description: Mortgage rates held steady this week, keeping the average long-term U.S. home loan rate at its highest level in nearly three years. The benchmark 30-year fixed-rate mortgage was unchanged from last week at 7.40%, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said Thursday. One year ago, the average rate was 6.27%. The latest reading ends a seven-week climb for the average rate, which is at the highest level since Nov. 16, 2023, when it was at 7.44%. Meanwhile, borrowing costs on 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, often sought by borrowers refinancing a home loan, eased this week. That average rate dropped to 6.71% from 6.73% last week. A year ago, it was at 5.52%. Rates on home loans are influenced by inflation, Federal Reserve policy and bond-market investors’ expectations for the economy, among other factors. They generally follow the trajectory of the 10-year Treasury yield, which lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans. Mortgage rates have been climbing since late February, when the U.S. war with Iran began, pushing up the price of oil and driving inflation higher. The run-up in rates also reflects heightened bond market volatility, which has pushed up yields on U.S. Treasurys. U.S. home sales remain stalled this year in large part because of rising mortgage rates, which can add hundreds of dollars a month in costs for borrowers, limiting homebuyers’ purchasing power and prompting many to put off buying a home. The recent string of mortgage rate increases snapped as the 10-year Treasury yield pulled back from its highest level since 2002. The yield was at 5.10% at midday Thursday on the bond market. It had topped 5.30% earlier this month amid worries about high inflation, signals of a strong U.S. economy and other factors. It’s still well above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran began. In late February, the average rate on a 30-year mortgage briefly dipped to 5.98%, its lowest level going back to late 2022. The 1.42 percentage point increase in the rate since then translates roughly into an additional monthly cost of $376 for a borrower financing a $400,000 home loan at the current average rate. Depending on a borrower’s income, credit and other factors, they may qualify for a rate on a 30-year mortgage that is below or above the current average. The U.S. housing market has been in a slump since 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. This week, the National Association of Realtors said that existing U.S. home sales rose in September from the previous month, but slowed compared to a year earlier amid rising mortgage rates and home prices. The surge in mortgage rates in recent weeks has put off many would-be homebuyers. Mortgage applications, which include loans to buy a home or refinance an existing mortgage, fell 2.7% last week from the previous week as mortgage rates rose, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association. Faced with higher borrowing costs due to rising mortgage rates, more homebuyers are opting for adjustable-rate mortgages, or ARMs. Such loans, which typically offer lower initial interest rates than traditional 30-year, fixed-rate mortgages, accounted for 10.5% of all mortgage applications last week — the highest level in a year, MBA said. Despite holding steady this week, it’s likely that the recent upward march in mortgage rates is not over. Reports this week showing prices at the consumer and wholesale level rose more than economists expected flashed the latest sign that inflation has worsened as rising oil prices add on costs to all manner of goods and services. The reports could persuade the inflation-fighters at the Federal Reserve to hike their key interest rate by December, and could set the stage for more rate increases early next year, said Jiayi Xu, a senior economist at Realtor.com. “In other words, mortgage rates are unlikely to ease anytime soon, but bringing inflation under control would pave the way for lower rates and a much-needed boost to affordability for the year ahead,” Xu said. Wall Street traders now expect the Fed will keep its short-term rate unchanged at its next policy meeting this month, but the odds of a rate increase in December have jumped to 64.6% from 49.9% a month ago, according to data from the CME Group. While the central bank doesn’t set mortgage rates, its decisions to raise or lower its short-term rate are watched closely by bond investors and can ultimately affect the yield on 10-year Treasurys. In its latest forecast, mortgage buyer Fannie Mae projects that the rate on a 30-year mortgage will average 7.4% in the final quarter of this year and average 7.5% in 2027.

headlines.title: Preliminary 2.5 magnitude earthquake strikes near Gilroy
headlines.description: A preliminary 2.5 magnitude earthquake struck near Gilroy late Thursday morning, according to the United States Geological Survey. The quake hit at 10:57 a.m. and was centered 6.1 miles east-southeast of Gilroy, 9.9 miles north-northwest of Hollister and 14.5 miles southeast of Morgan Hill, the USGS said. This is a developing story. Details may change as more information becomes available. Stay tuned for updates. headlines.title: Testimony begins in Sheng Thao corruption trial
headlines.description: Testimony is underway in the federal corruption trial of former Oakland Mayor Sheng Thao. Leigh Hanson, Thao’s former chief of staff in 2023, testified about the oversized role Thao’s longtime boyfriend and co-defendant, Andre Jones, had in her administration despite not being a city employee. Hanson said Jones appeared uninvited on a Zoom interview for an important role in the administration. Hanson also testified that Jones threatened her job as chief of staff after she walked out of a meeting with Jones, the mayor and the city attorney because she believed Jones’ presence as a non-employee would jeopardize attorney-client privilege. Jones allegedly told Hanson afterward, “We’ll see which one is left at the end of the day.” Hanson was fired by Thao’s interim successor after Thao was recalled. Sheng Thao Oct 13 Sheng Thao Oct 13 Sheng Thao 21 hours ago Sheng Thao Jul 30 Federal prosecutors have indicted Thao on charges of bribery, conspiracy and wire fraud, along with Jones and David and Andy Duong. The Duongs own California Waste Solutions, Oakland’s recycling contractor. Federal prosecutors allege Thao helped the company secure future contracts with the city of Oakland in exchange for helping her get elected mayor and payments to Jones. Thao and her co-defendants have pleaded not guilty to all charges. Hanson also testified about Thao overruling her and hiring Larry Gallegos as deputy director of housing, even though Hanson did not believe Gallegos was the right fit. Prosecutors allege Thao would use Gallegos to have the city buy 100 housing units from Evolutionary Homes, one of the companies at the center of the alleged bribery scheme involving the Duongs. Thursday marks the first day of testimony in the corruption trial, with Hanson the first of 68 potential witnesses federal prosecutors could call.

headlines.title: PG&E power shutoffs affect more than 6,000 Bay Area customers
headlines.description: PG&E had shut off power to 6,824 customers in five Bay Area counties as of Thursday morning as a safety measure ahead of forecasted high winds and dry conditions. PG&E said that as of 6 a.m., the outages affected 3,158 customers in Napa County, 2,169 in Sonoma County, 1,358 in Contra Costa County, 88 in Alameda County and 51 in Solano County. In Mendocino County, there were 444 affected customers. PG&E began shutting off power around 5:30 p.m. Wednesday as part of a Public Safety Power Shutoff. About 90,000 customers across 29 counties are included in the shutoffs, the utility said. More power shutoffs were planned for Thursday morning and Friday morning. PG&E said affected customers had received multiple notifications about the service interruptions. The utility plans to open more than 40 Community Resource Centers across 25 counties. The centers will offer device charging, Wi-Fi, bottled water, snacks and other supplies.

headlines.title: SFPD cancels remembrance event for retired Deputy Chief Ann Mannix
headlines.description: The San Francisco Police Department canceled a remembrance event honoring retired Deputy Chief Ann Mannix that was scheduled for Thursday. “We are deeply grateful for everyone’s outpouring of support during this difficult time,” the department said in a statement Wednesday night. Mannix, 65, her husband, retired Officer Kevin Mannix, 68, and their daughter, Katherine Elizabeth Mannix, 24, were found dead at their home in unincorporated Marin County on Sunday. Authorities are investigating the deaths as a suspected double-murder suicide. Kevin Mannix fatally shot his wife and daughter before shooting himself, according to the preliminary investigation by the Marin County Sheriff’s Office. Ann Mannix served with the San Francisco Police Department for more than 30 years. She worked at several district stations and in the department’s Special Operations and Field Operations bureaus. She was the first woman to lead the department’s tactical company, Police Chief Derrick Lew said. Lew previously expressed condolences to the Mannix family, friends and colleagues, saying the department was grieving and trying to process the tragedy. Mayor Daniel Lurie also praised Mannix’s decades of service to San Francisco, calling her a trailblazer who became the first woman to join and lead the department’s SWAT team.

headlines.title: Owner Joe Lacob believed in Valkyries from Day 1, but reaching WNBA Finals in second year remarkable
headlines.description: The moment Joe Lacob walks into the Chase Center and heads for his courtside seats, he and his family immediately feel the enormous energy and wholesome vibe that is the Golden State Valkyries’ “Ballhalla” home crowd game after game, sellout after violet-crazed sellout. The women’s basketball franchise Lacob always envisioned while owning the Golden State Warriors has come together in no time, and in all the right ways – from relatable players other teams overlooked to leadership from the top down and smart branding complete with a beloved raven “bestie” Violet. Just don’t dare calling her a mascot. On Saturday, Lacob will be there roaring with the rest of them as his Valkyries begin their quest for a WNBA championship in just their second year of existence. And whatever happens, he is immensely proud of the progress and the loyal support from everyone representing all walks of life who contributes to one of the best home-court advantages anywhere. “What is truly remarkable is how great our fans are. Our players love it, we love it,” Lacob said. “It’s great, it’s a cohesion, it’s everybody coming together all at the same time and rooting for something that is new and fresh and it’s timely. And people see it and feel it. What’s going on in that arena is fantastic, it’s remarkable, it’s incredibly fun. “I love walking in there, my wife, my family, we all love walking in there to the tremendous feeling of camaraderie and togetherness. We all as a team of people, fans, players, organization, together we’re making history and we all feel it.” Owner tries to back up his bold prediction For decades, Lacob has loved women’s basketball and when he brought a WNBA franchise to the Bay Area at last, the owner had no hesitations about making bold predictions. He promised a championship within the first five years. And now in the second year the Valkyries are playing for one. “I’m telling you right now, we will win a WNBA championship in the first five years of this franchise,” Lacob declared on Oct. 5, 2023, when the WNBA announced Lacob’s ownership group had been awarded an expansion franchise. “I think it just goes to show that with a new team, (you can have success) with a clear vision of what you want and the identity that you want,” center Kiah Stokes said. “Shoutout to the Valkyries organization, because they had this vision from the start, and to be able to see it come to fruition already in year two is pretty amazing and pretty special. We have a great group, it’s really special, and we’re looking forward to the finals.” Lacob had followed his prediction with the same statement to now-coach Natalie Nakase when he interviewed her to be the sideline leader. She was all in from that moment. “It’s just a perfect confluence of events and people and experience and timing. It’s just a lot of things that have all come together at the right time,” Lacob said. “I’m not going to sit here and tell you that I am shocked by this, I’m not. I think all the ingredients were there and I made that prediction knowingly and understood what I was saying, now to do it in two years, no one could sit here and tell you that would be something they would predict. No one, not even me.” Many of the Valkyries have taken unsung paths Under Lacob’s leadership and the hiring of President Jess Smith and her staff, Golden State has built a roster of understated stars. Veronica Burton got cut by Dallas two years ago, while her backup point guard Kaitlyn Chen was briefly let go by the Valkyries last season before she returned. Kayla Thornton is a 33-year-old undrafted forward out of the University of Texas El Paso who became an All-Star in 2025. Gabby Williams had something to prove in the WNBA after sensing others didn’t believe in her ability. That’s not the case anymore. “It feels special because this is a special group,” Williams said. “All we need is each other. We just need to believe in each other, we know we weren’t a team that was talked about, but just the culture and going to work every day, we felt that we had something worth fighting for. That’s how we’re going into the finals, with that same mentality — staying together and staying unselfish.” Lacob is into it, yelling from courtside in his Valkyries violet gear. But this goes back decades for him. He supported Stanford and followed along when Hall of Fame Cardinal coach Tara VanDerveer led the Americans’ gold-medal dominance at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics and Lacob became a founding owner of the San Jose Lasers in the former ABL. He is thrilled with the WNBA’s recent strides and the rise of women’s sports. NBA pros have become huge fans, too Count Warriors coach Steve Kerr as a huge fan of these Valkyries. “They’re so fun to watch, they’re so unselfish, they’re so tough, smart, well coached,” Kerr said. “And having watched this thing unfold over two years, I can’t imagine that there’s ever been a better expansion team in terms of the unveiling of everything – the brand, the colors, the name, the logo, the mascot, the vibe in the building. It’s incredible. We’re really proud of the team, excited for Natalie and her staff. We can’t wait for the finals.” It certainly helps to have Stephen Curry, Draymond Green, Brandin Podziemski and Gui Santos showing up in support. Kyrie Irving has taken notice, too. No matter who is cheering, Nakase has a message for the loyal, loud fans in a home crowd of 18,064 — including her top boss, Lacob — she is so counting on bringing their support to another level. “Since we’re prepping for a great game plan, Ballhalla better be prepping for a game plan,” Nakase said. “So as soon as they’re announced, I need some hostility. If they do a challenge, I need hostility, and if they’re shooting free throws, I need that thing to be rocking. Game plan, Ballhalla, get ready, get prepped.” ___ See AP’s full WNBA coverage here

headlines.title: Black Panther Party stalwarts to celebrate 1966 founding in Oakland, programs that aided the poor
headlines.description: The legacy of the Black Panther Party lives on six decades after its founding, in the work of a Seattle medical center started to address systemic health disparities in the African American community, particularly among Black children. Originally known as the Sidney Miller Free Medical Clinic in 1969, it put into practice the national Black Panther Party’s Ten-Point Program to uplift African Americans as the Black Power movement gained momentum. Now, as the Carolyn Downs Family Medical Center, it, along with the affiliated Country Doctor Community Clinic, sees tens of thousands of patients in a year. As the celebration begins Thursday for the Black Panther Party’s Oct. 15, 1966, founding in Oakland, California, former members are looking beyond the iconic black leather jackets, berets and clenched fists to highlight programs aimed at healing disenfranchised and forgotten communities. From free medical clinics and pushing nationally for sickle cell anemia testing to providing free breakfasts for children and community schools promoting education and literacy, the Black Panthers understood what was needed during the racially turbulent 1960s, said Fredrika Newton, widow of co-founder Huey P. Newton. “We sought to meet the basic needs of the Black community, not only the Black, but all oppressed communities,” she told The Associated Press Tuesday. “Children were going to school hungry. People couldn’t get medical care. People were sleeping in the streets, just like today.” A planned four-day conference this weekend in downtown Oakland includes a gala. Surviving original members and other Black Panther Party veterans are expected to attend. Pushing for Black empowerment and against racist policing Co-founders Huey P. Newton and Bobby Seale were students at Merritt College in Oakland, where they formed the Panthers during the Civil Rights Movement. Both became active in Bay Area politics during the mid-1960s and believed the Civil Rights movement may have addressed the plight of Blacks in Southern states, but it failed to bring about any real change in the U.S. West and North. With Newton as minister of defense and Seale as the group’s chair, the Black Panther Party for Self-Defense advocated for political and economic empowerment and initiatives to improve life for the city’s Black residents in addition to standing up to what they saw as racist and heavy-handed policing in the Black community. “We knew that Black people were getting brutalized by the police,” said Fredrika Newton, who joined the Black Panther Party in 1971 after meeting Huey P. Newton. “We wanted to make sure that they were getting educated and taught how to protect themselves.” Confrontations with law enforcement — broadcast to households across the country — galvanized Black support for the organization but also worried many white people. Seale, declaring that the Second Amendment right to bear arms also applied to Blacks, led a small group of armed Panthers in 1967 into the California state legislature. The Black Panther Party was targeted by the FBI, which put its leaders and members under surveillance and operated a yearslong disruption and discrediting campaign. John “Bunchy” Crear was caught up in the maelstrom of race and politics sweeping across California in the late 1960s and early 1970s. Crear, along with some friends, began attending Black Panther political education classes in 1970. He joined at age 19. “I was at home in my bedroom listening to my music when my mother comes in and says two white gentlemen from the FBI were in the living room wanting to talk to me,” recalled Crear, 74, who lives in Houston. “I walked in and there were the men in black. They asked if I was a member of the Black Panther Party, then pulled a book out with photos asking if I knew this person, if I knew that person.” “’Well, John, if you stay in school and get you a good job, you’ll never hear from us again,’” Crear said the men told him before leaving. Healthcare part of community survival programs The Black Panther Party purchased buildings and homes that served as safe houses and centers for their community survival programs, which mostly addressed food insecurity, lack of healthcare, unequal education and other issues in Black communities. Chapters were started in about 70 other cities. The chapter in Seattle started one of the 13 original Black Panther Party-founded healthcare clinics across the country and is the only one still in operation. “Thinking especially about Black folks in the 1960s and 70s, it was impossible to try to address one need and not all because they were vulnerable and under threat in so many areas,” said Brandy Taylor, chief executive of the Carolyn Downs Family Medical Center and Country Doctor Community Clinic. “It wasn’t just about medical care. It was about free speech, social services, food security and knowing your rights. There were so many doors closed that you couldn’t survive without addressing them all,” she said. From the end to emulation The Black Panther Party folded in 1982 after years of police surveillance, as well as dwindling national membership, infighting, allegations of embezzlement and scandals in which Huey P. Newton was implicated and criminally charged. Newton’s addictions to alcohol and drugs overtook him. He was murdered in Oakland, California, in 1989 by a drug dealer. In 2021, a bronze bust of Huey P. Newton was unveiled in Oakland. However, some see similarities in why the Black Panthers were started with the emergence of the Black Lives Matter movement following the 2013 acquittal of the man who killed Trayvon Martin, a Black teenager in Sanford, Florida. “We want to let young people know exactly what we did and what could be done,” said Fredrika Newton, who also is president and co-founder of the Huey P. Newton Foundation. “This is not a blueprint for what they can do now, but they can certainly see what we did, take what we did, apply them to the conditions today and organize,” she said. “Organize around the needs that exist today.” _____________ Williams is a Detroit-based member of AP’s Race & Ethnicity team.

headlines.title: Pet emu runs loose in Santa Cruz before being corralled
headlines.description: Authorities in Santa Cruz recently responded to an unusual call of an emu running in and out of traffic. The California Highway Patrol said it received several calls about the giant bird running into traffic near Harper Street and 17th Avenue. “While we often deal with dogs, cats, deer, and occasionally birds, an Emu was unexpected!” CHP Santa Cruz said in a social media post. The CHP said the emu’s owner quickly came out and was able to corral their feathery pet.
